text: {"domains":{"block_M":[32,64,128],"block_N":[64,128],"block_K":[32,64],"num_stages":[1,2,3],"threads":[128]},"shared_memory_limit":32768,"weights":{"traffic":1,"launches":0.5,"pipeline":2,"footprint":1.25},"rationale":"Five attempts compiled, passed numerical checks on the exact source/TIR, and completed GB10 simulation (estimates only; no CUDA binary executed, no hardware measurement). Best remains attempt-01 (64,64,64,2) at 156.26us smem 32768 proxy 3.384; others: (128,64,64,1) 157.05us, (64,64,32,3) 157.63us smem 24576, (128,64,32,2) 157.80us, (64,128,64,1) 157.30us. Every block_N=128 probe (attempt-04) and the only stage-3 probe (attempt-02) underperformed the (64,64,64,2) point, so the analytic proxy is clearly not monotone with simulated latency; ranking stays cautious and no global optimality is claimed. Observations: stage-2 mixes lead; block_K=32 at stages 2-3 regressed, suggesting block_K=64 is the productive K-tile; block_N=128 did not help despite the tall-N shape, so traffic is eased from 1.5 to 1.0 to stop over-rewarding wide-N tuples. Pipeline kept at 2 (stage-2 is the current leader) and footprint raised to 1.25 to discourage the cap-saturating 32768-byte tiles that dominate attempts 00/01/03/04, favoring tuples that leave headroom. Launches lowered to 0.5 since launch counts remain small relative to traffic/pipeline for this wide-M tall-N shape. Domains remain fully nonempty and feasible (block_M divides 128; block_N and block_K divide 4096; threads fixed 128), so HiGHS still owns tuple selection and explores unmeasured points; shared-memory limit kept at 32768 (portability cap). Next hypothesis: untested (block_M=32 or 128, block_N=64, block_K=64, num_stages=2) or (32,128,64,2) tuples may beat the (64,64,64,2) leader now that footprint pressure favors sub-cap tiles and traffic/launch pressure is reduced; verify compiled smem and Metal-executed source/TIR, and treat simulated_us as a ranking proxy only, never as hardware latency."}
